-- ============================================
-- COMPREHENSIVE CRUD TESTING FRAMEWORK
-- ============================================

-- 1. SETUP: Create test environment
CREATE TABLE test_results (
    test_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    operation VARCHAR(20),
    test_scenario VARCHAR(100),
    expected_result VARCHAR(50),
    actual_result VARCHAR(50),
    passed BOOLEAN,
    test_time TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- 2. TEST DATA SETUP
CREATE TABLE test_users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    username VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'active',
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP,
    deleted_at TIMESTAMP
);

-- 3. CREATE OPERATION TESTS
-- Test 3.1: Valid creation
INSERT INTO test_users (username, email) 
VALUES ('test_user_1', 'test1@example.com');

INSERT INTO test_results (operation, test_scenario, expected_result, actual_result, passed)
SELECT 
    'CREATE',
    'Valid user creation',
    'User exists with correct data',
    CASE 
        WHEN COUNT(*) = 1 AND username = 'test_user_1' THEN 'User created correctly'
        ELSE 'Creation failed or data incorrect'
    END,
    COUNT(*) = 1 AND username = 'test_user_1'
FROM test_users WHERE email = 'test1@example.com';

-- Test 3.2: Duplicate prevention
INSERT INTO test_results (operation, test_scenario, expected_result, actual_result, passed)
SELECT 
    'CREATE',
    'Duplicate email prevention',
    'Second insert should fail',
    CASE 
        WHEN EXISTS (
            SELECT 1 FROM test_users 
            WHERE email = 'test1@example.com'
            GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
        ) THEN 'Duplicate allowed (BUG!)'
        ELSE 'Duplicate prevented (GOOD)'
    END,
    NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM test_users 
        WHERE email = 'test1@example.com'
        GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
    )
FROM test_users;

-- 4. READ OPERATION TESTS
-- Test 4.1: Basic read
INSERT INTO test_results (operation, test_scenario, expected_result, actual_result, passed)
SELECT 
    'READ',
    'Basic user retrieval',
    'Retrieve user by ID',
    CASE 
        WHEN username = 'test_user_1' THEN 'User retrieved correctly'
        ELSE 'User not found or wrong data'
    END,
    username = 'test_user_1'
FROM test_users WHERE email = 'test1@example.com';

-- Test 4.2: Read non-existent
INSERT INTO test_results (operation, test_scenario, expected_result, actual_result, passed)
SELECT 
    'READ',
    'Read non-existent user',
    'Should return no results',
    CASE 
        WHEN COUNT(*) = 0 THEN 'No results (correct)'
        ELSE 'Found non-existent user (BUG!)'
    END,
    COUNT(*) = 0
FROM test_users WHERE id = 999999;

-- 5. UPDATE OPERATION TESTS
-- Test 5.1: Valid update
UPDATE test_users 
SET username = 'updated_user', updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE email = 'test1@example.com';

INSERT INTO test_results (operation, test_scenario, expected_result, actual_result, passed)
SELECT 
    'UPDATE',
    'Basic user update',
    'Username updated, timestamp changed',
    CASE 
        WHEN username = 'updated_user' AND updated_at IS NOT NULL 
        THEN 'Update successful'
        ELSE 'Update failed or incomplete'
    END,
    username = 'updated_user' AND updated_at IS NOT NULL
FROM test_users WHERE email = 'test1@example.com';

-- Test 5.2: Update non-existent
INSERT INTO test_results (operation, test_scenario, expected_result, actual_result, passed)
SELECT 
    'UPDATE',
    'Update non-existent user',
    'Should affect 0 rows',
    CASE 
        WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM test_users WHERE id = 999999) 
        THEN 'No rows affected (correct)'
        ELSE 'Updated non-existent user (BUG!)'
    END,
    NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM test_users WHERE id = 999999)
FROM test_users;

-- 6. DELETE OPERATION TESTS
-- Test 6.1: Soft delete
UPDATE test_users 
SET deleted_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE email = 'test1@example.com';

INSERT INTO test_results (operation, test_scenario, expected_result, actual_result, passed)
SELECT 
    'DELETE',
    'Soft delete user',
    'User marked as deleted but still in table',
    CASE 
        WHEN deleted_at IS NOT NULL THEN 'Soft deleted correctly'
        ELSE 'Not deleted (BUG!)'
    END,
    deleted_at IS NOT NULL
FROM test_users WHERE email = 'test1@example.com';

-- 7. RESULTS REPORT
SELECT 
    operation,
    test_scenario,
    expected_result,
    actual_result,
    CASE WHEN passed THEN '✅ PASS' ELSE '❌ FAIL' END as result
FROM test_results 
ORDER BY operation, test_time;

-- 8. CLEANUP
DROP TABLE test_results;
DROP TABLE test_users;

-- ============================================
-- This framework:
-- 1. Tests all CRUD operations
-- 2. Records results for tracking
-- 3. Includes edge cases
-- 4. Easy to extend
-- 5. Self-documenting
-- ============================================

content.caption: Automated CRUD Testing Script
content.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Automated CRUD Testing Framework
Tests Create, Read, Update, Delete operations end-to-end
"""

import sqlite3
import time
from typing import Dict, List, Optional
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime

@dataclass
class TestResult:
    operation: str
    scenario: str
    passed: bool
    details: str
    duration_ms: float

def create_test_database() -> sqlite3.Connection:
    """Create a fresh test database"""
    conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')  # In-memory for testing
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    
    # Create test tables
    cursor.execute('''
    CREATE TABLE users (
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
        username TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
        email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
        status TEXT DEFAULT 'active',
        created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
        updated_at TIMESTAMP,
        deleted_at TIMESTAMP
    )
    ''')
    
    cursor.execute('''
    CREATE TABLE orders (
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
        user_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
        total_amount DECIMAL(10,2),
        status TEXT DEFAULT 'pending',
        FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
    )
    ''')
    
    conn.commit()
    return conn

def test_create_operations(conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> List[TestResult]:
    """Test CREATE operations"""
    results = []
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    
    # Test 1: Valid user creation
    start = time.time()
    try:
        cursor.execute(
            "INSERT INTO users (username, email) VALUES (?, ?)",
            ("test_user", "test@example.com")
        )
        conn.commit()
        
        # Verify creation
        cursor.execute(
            "SELECT username, email, status FROM users WHERE email = ?",
            ("test@example.com",)
        )
        user = cursor.fetchone()
        
        passed = user and user[0] == "test_user" and user[1] == "test@example.com"
        details = f"Created user: {user}" if user else "User not found"
        
    except Exception as e:
        passed = False
        details = f"Error: {e}"
    
    results.append(TestResult(
        operation="CREATE",
        scenario="Valid user creation",
        passed=passed,
        details=details,
        duration_ms=(time.time() - start) * 1000
    ))
    
    # Test 2: Duplicate prevention
    start = time.time()
    try:
        cursor.execute(
            "INSERT INTO users (username, email) VALUES (?, ?)",
            ("duplicate_user", "test@example.com")  # Same email
        )
        conn.commit()
        passed = False  # Should have failed
        details = "Duplicate allowed (BUG!)"
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
        passed = True
        details = "Duplicate prevented (correct)"
    except Exception as e:
        passed = False
        details = f"Unexpected error: {e}"
    
    results.append(TestResult(
        operation="CREATE",
        scenario="Duplicate email prevention",
        passed=passed,
        details=details,
        duration_ms=(time.time() - start) * 1000
    ))
    
    return results

def test_read_operations(conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> List[TestResult]:
    """Test READ operations"""
    results = []
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    
    # Test 1: Read existing user
    start = time.time()
    try:
        cursor.execute(
            "SELECT id, username, email FROM users WHERE email = ?",
            ("test@example.com",)
        )
        user = cursor.fetchone()
        
        passed = user is not None
        details = f"Found user: {user}" if user else "User not found"
        
    except Exception as e:
        passed = False
        details = f"Error: {e}"
    
    results.append(TestResult(
        operation="READ",
        scenario="Read existing user",
        passed=passed,
        details=details,
        duration_ms=(time.time() - start) * 1000
    ))
    
    # Test 2: Read non-existent user
    start = time.time()
    try:
        cursor.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?",
            ("nonexistent@example.com",)
        )
        user = cursor.fetchone()
        
        passed = user is None
        details = "No results found (correct)" if user is None else "Found non-existent user (BUG!)"
        
    except Exception as e:
        passed = False
        details = f"Error: {e}"
    
    results.append(TestResult(
        operation="READ",
        scenario="Read non-existent user",
        passed=passed,
        details=details,
        duration_ms=(time.time() - start) * 1000
    ))
    
    return results

def test_update_operations(conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> List[TestResult]:
    """Test UPDATE operations"""
    results = []
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    
    # Test 1: Update user status
    start = time.time()
    try:
        cursor.execute(
            "UPDATE users SET status = ?, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE email = ?",
            ("inactive", "test@example.com")
        )
        conn.commit()
        
        # Verify update
        cursor.execute(
            "SELECT status, updated_at FROM users WHERE email = ?",
            ("test@example.com",)
        )
        user = cursor.fetchone()
        
        passed = user and user[0] == "inactive" and user[1] is not None
        details = f"Updated user: status={user[0]}, updated_at={user[1]}" if user else "Update failed"
        
    except Exception as e:
        passed = False
        details = f"Error: {e}"
    
    results.append(TestResult(
        operation="UPDATE",
        scenario="Update user status",
        passed=passed,
        details=details,
        duration_ms=(time.time() - start) * 1000
    ))
    
    return results

def test_delete_operations(conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> List[TestResult]:
    """Test DELETE operations"""
    results = []
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    
    # Test 1: Soft delete user
    start = time.time()
    try:
        cursor.execute(
            "UPDATE users SET deleted_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE email = ?",
            ("test@example.com",)
        )
        conn.commit()
        
        # Verify soft delete
        cursor.execute(
            "SELECT deleted_at FROM users WHERE email = ?",
            ("test@example.com",)
        )
        deleted_at = cursor.fetchone()[0]
        
        passed = deleted_at is not None
        details = f"Soft deleted at: {deleted_at}" if passed else "Not deleted"
        
    except Exception as e:
        passed = False
        details = f"Error: {e}"
    
    results.append(TestResult(
        operation="DELETE",
        scenario="Soft delete user",
        passed=passed,
        details=details,
        duration_ms=(time.time() - start) * 1000
    ))
    
    return results

def run_crud_test_suite():
    """Run complete CRUD test suite"""
    print("🚀 Starting CRUD Test Suite\n")
    
    # Create fresh test database
    conn = create_test_database()
    
    # Run all test suites
    all_results = []
    
    print("📝 Testing CREATE Operations...")
    all_results.extend(test_create_operations(conn))
    
    print("🔍 Testing READ Operations...")
    all_results.extend(test_read_operations(conn))
    
    print("✏️  Testing UPDATE Operations...")
    all_results.extend(test_update_operations(conn))
    
    print("🗑️  Testing DELETE Operations...")
    all_results.extend(test_delete_operations(conn))
    
    # Close connection
    conn.close()
    
    # Print results
    print("\n📊 TEST RESULTS:")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    passed_count = sum(1 for r in all_results if r.passed)
    total_count = len(all_results)
    
    for result in all_results:
        status = "✅ PASS" if result.passed else "❌ FAIL"
        print(f"{status} [{result.operation}] {result.scenario}")
        print(f"   Details: {result.details}")
        print(f"   Duration: {result.duration_ms:.1f}ms\n")
    
    print("=" * 80)
    print(f"🎯 Summary: {passed_count}/{total_count} tests passed ({passed_count/total_count*100:.1f}%)")
    
    if passed_count == total_count:
        print("🌟 All CRUD operations working correctly!")
    else:
        print("⚠️  Some CRUD operations need attention.")
    
    return all_results

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_crud_test_suite()

content.title: Testing CRUD in Distributed Systems
content.explanation:
Modern applications aren't single databases—they're distributed systems. CRUD operations span multiple services, databases, caches, and queues. This introduces new failure modes.

**Distributed CRUD challenges:**

1. **Eventual consistency**: Write to service A, read from service B
2. **Network partitions**: Services can't talk to each other
3. **Dual writes**: Updating two systems simultaneously
4. **Idempotency**: Retries creating duplicate data
5. **Ordering guarantees**: Which update happened first?

**Testing patterns for distributed CRUD:**

**Pattern 1: Eventual consistency verification**
```sql
-- After creating user in main service
-- Wait for replication to read replica

SELECT 
    NOW() as current_time,
    (SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM users) as last_created,
    CASE 
        WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users_replica) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users)
        THEN '✓ Replicated'
        ELSE '✗ Replication lag'
    END as replication_status
FROM dual;

-- Monitor until consistent or timeout
```

**Pattern 2: Idempotency testing**
```sql
-- Test retry behavior
-- Send same create request twice with same idempotency key

SELECT 
    request_id,
    COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) as distinct_users_created,
    CASE 
        WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) = 1 THEN '✓ Idempotent'
        ELSE '✗ Not idempotent (duplicate users)'
    END as idempotency_status
FROM api_requests 
WHERE idempotency_key = 'test_key_123'
GROUP BY request_id;
```

**Pattern 3: Cross-service transaction testing**
```sql
-- Creating order should:
-- 1. Create order in orders service
-- 2. Reserve inventory in inventory service
-- 3. Create payment in payment service

-- Verify all services consistent
SELECT 
    'Orders' as service,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE user_id = 123) as count
UNION ALL
SELECT 
    'Inventory reserves',
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM inventory_reserves WHERE order_id IN 
        (SELECT id FROM orders WHERE user_id = 123))
UNION ALL
SELECT 
    'Payments',
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments WHERE order_id IN 
        (SELECT id FROM orders WHERE user_id = 123));

-- All counts should match (or follow business rules)
```

**Distributed CRUD testing principles:**
1. **Test failure modes**: What happens when network fails mid-operation?
2. **Test recovery**: Can the system recover to consistent state?
3. **Test latency**: How long until consistency achieved?
4. **Test ordering**: Are there race conditions between services?
5. **Test monitoring**: Can you detect when consistency breaks?

In distributed systems, CRUD isn't atomic. Your tests shouldn't assume it is.

content.title: The CRUD Testing Manifesto
content.explanation:
**We test CRUD operations because:**

1. **Data is precious** - Users trust us with their information
2. **Operations are foundational** - Everything else builds on CRUD
3. **Failures are costly** - In money, time, and trust
4. **Bugs are predictable** - We know where to look
5. **Testing is preventive** - We find issues before users do

**Our testing principles:**

1. **Verify, don't assume** - Check database state, not just API responses
2. **Test boundaries** - Minimum, maximum, null, invalid
3. **Test concurrently** - Real users don't wait their turn
4. **Test completely** - All fields, all side effects, all related data
5. **Test failure** - Graceful degradation is a feature
6. **Document patterns** - Reusable tests save time
7. **Automate systematically** - Consistent verification across releases
8. **Measure coverage** - Know what you're testing and what you're missing

**The ultimate goal:**
Not just to find bugs, but to build confidence. Confidence that:
• User data is safe
• Business operations work
• The system is reliable
• Trust is earned

Every CRUD test you write, every bug you find, every edge case you consider—it all adds up to a more trustworthy system.

Start with one CRUD operation. Test it thoroughly. Learn the patterns. Apply them to the next. Soon, you'll be the person who knows the data flows better than anyone. The person who prevents the data disasters before they happen.

That's the power of CRUD testing. It's not glamorous. But it's essential. And it's where real testing impact happens.

content.title: The Migration Minefield: Why Moving Data is the Riskiest Thing You'll Do
Data Migration: The Silent Killer of Projects
content.explanation:
Data migration is like performing heart transplant surgery while the patient is running a marathon. You're moving the most critical organ of your business—its data—from one body to another, while the business keeps operating.

**Why migrations fail spectacularly:**

1. **The 'Works in Dev' Delusion**: "It worked with 100 test records!" → Production has 10 million.
2. **The 'Just a Copy' Fallacy**: "We're just moving data" → Forgetting transformations, relationships, business rules.
3. **The 'We'll Fix It Live' Gambit**: "Minor data issues can be cleaned up after" → Becomes months of manual corrections.
4. **The 'Nobody Will Notice' Assumption**: Small discrepancies in historical data → Breaks reporting, analytics, compliance.

**Real migration disasters:**
• **Bank merger**: 2% of accounts got wrong balances → $47M in incorrect transactions
• **Healthcare system upgrade**: Patient allergies didn't migrate → Wrong medications prescribed
• **E-commerce replatform**: Product categories scrambled → 40% drop in sales for 3 months
• **Government system**: 15 years of tax records 'migrated' → 30% incomplete, audit nightmare

Data migration testing isn't about checking if data moved. It's about verifying that MEANING moved. That business logic survived. That relationships stayed intact. That history remained accurate.

Because when data arrives broken at its destination, you don't just have a technical problem. You have a business crisis.

content.title: The Cost of Migration Failure
content.explanation:
Let's quantify what happens when data migration goes wrong:

**Direct financial costs:**
• **Extended downtime**: Business operations halt → Lost revenue per hour
• **Manual remediation**: Teams working 24/7 to fix data → Overtime, contractor costs
• **Regulatory fines**: GDPR, HIPAA violations → Millions in penalties
• **Legal settlements**: Wrong data causes harm → Lawsuits, settlements
• **Lost business**: Customers leave due to errors → Churn, lost lifetime value

**Indirect costs (often worse):**
• **Erosion of trust**: "They lost my data" → Brand damage for years
• **Operational paralysis**: "Which system has the truth?" → Decision paralysis
• **Technical debt**: Quick fixes become permanent → System fragility
• **Team burnout**: Emergency recovery mode → Talent loss
• **Project delays**: Everything else stops → Opportunity costs

**The testing ROI multiplier:**
Every hour spent testing migration:
• Prevents 10+ hours of emergency fixes
• Avoids 100+ hours of business disruption
• Saves potentially millions in costs
• Preserves customer trust (priceless)

Your migration tests are the insurance policy. The safety net. The proof that when you say "migration successful," you mean it. Not "mostly successful" or "successful except for those few issues." Actually successful.

Because in data migration, 'mostly' isn't good enough. 'Perfect' is the only acceptable outcome.

content.title: The Migration Testing Mindset
content.explanation:
Developers think about migration: "Move data from A to B."
Testers think about migration: "Preserve TRUTH from A to B."

It's a fundamental difference in perspective:

**The developer's checklist:**
• Extract data from source
• Transform as needed
• Load into destination
• Handle errors
• Report completion

**The tester's checklist:**
• **Before migration**: What's the current state of truth?
• **During migration**: Is every transformation correct and reversible?
• **After migration**: Does the new state match the old state in MEANING?
• **Long-term**: Does the migrated data support all business processes?

**Example: Migrating user accounts**

Developer tests: Count of users matches

Tester tests:
1. **Count matches** (obvious)
2. **Each user's data is accurate** (all fields, transformed correctly)
3. **Relationships preserved** (user → orders → order items)
4. **Business rules still work** (active users can order, suspended can't)
5. **Historical data intact** (old orders still accessible)
6. **Security preserved** (passwords hashed, permissions maintained)
7. **Performance acceptable** (queries still fast with migrated data)
8. **Edge cases handled** (users with special characters, null values, duplicates)
9. **Rollback possible** (if something's wrong, we can go back)
10. **Monitoring in place** (we'll know if issues appear later)

Migration testing isn't a phase. It's a continuous verification of truth preservation. From the first record to the last, from the simplest field to the most complex relationship.

Your job isn't to test that data moved. Your job is to prove that truth survived.

content.caption: Basic Migration Verification Queries
content.code:
-- ============================================
-- MIGRATION VERIFICATION 101
-- The essential checks every migration needs
-- ============================================

-- 1. COUNT VERIFICATION: Did we get everything?
-- Most basic check - but not sufficient alone
SELECT 
    'Source' as system,
    COUNT(*) as total_records
FROM legacy.users
UNION ALL
SELECT 
    'Destination' as system,
    COUNT(*) as total_records
FROM new_system.users;
-- Should match exactly (or follow business rules)

-- 2. SAMPLE VERIFICATION: Is the data correct?
-- Compare random samples from source and destination
WITH source_sample AS (
    SELECT id, username, email, created_at
    FROM legacy.users
    WHERE MOD(id, 100) = 0  -- Sample every 100th record
    ORDER BY id
    LIMIT 100
),
dest_sample AS (
    SELECT legacy_id, username, email, created_at
    FROM new_system.users
    WHERE MOD(legacy_id, 100) = 0
    ORDER BY legacy_id
    LIMIT 100
)
SELECT 
    s.id as source_id,
    d.legacy_id as dest_id,
    CASE WHEN s.username = d.username THEN '✓' ELSE '✗' END as username_match,
    CASE WHEN s.email = d.email THEN '✓' ELSE '✗' END as email_match,
    CASE WHEN s.created_at = d.created_at THEN '✓' ELSE '✗' END as date_match
FROM source_sample s
JOIN dest_sample d ON s.id = d.legacy_id
WHERE s.username != d.username 
   OR s.email != d.email
   OR s.created_at != d.created_at;
-- Any rows returned = data corruption

-- 3. NULL CHECK: Did we lose required data?
SELECT 
    'Source NULLs' as check_type,
    COUNT(*) as count
FROM legacy.users 
WHERE email IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 
    'Destination NULLs',
    COUNT(*)
FROM new_system.users 
WHERE email IS NULL;
-- Should match (or destination should have fewer NULLs if cleaning)

-- 4. UNIQUENESS CHECK: Did we create duplicates?
SELECT 
    email,
    COUNT(*) as duplicate_count
FROM new_system.users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
-- Should be empty

-- 5. DATA RANGE CHECK: Are values still valid?
SELECT 
    'Invalid dates' as issue,
    COUNT(*) as count
FROM new_system.users
WHERE created_at > CURRENT_TIMESTAMP  -- Future dates
   OR created_at < '1990-01-01';      -- Too old

-- ============================================
-- PRO TIP: Run these BEFORE migration on test data
-- Then run DURING migration on subsets
-- Then run AFTER migration on everything
-- ============================================

content.title: The Three-Phase Migration Testing Strategy
content.explanation:
Effective migration testing happens in three overlapping phases, each with different goals and techniques:

**Phase 1: Pre-Migration Testing (The Rehearsal)**
**Goal**: Prove the migration process works before touching production data

**Activities:**
1. **Schema validation**: New system can hold all source data types
2. **Transformation testing**: Each data transformation verified with unit tests
3. **Volume testing**: Process works with production-sized data subsets
4. **Performance testing**: Migration completes within time windows
5. **Error handling**: Process handles bad data gracefully

**Key question**: "If we run this on production, will it work?"

**Phase 2: Migration Testing (The Performance)**
**Goal**: Verify actual migration as it happens

**Activities:**
1. **Parallel run**: Old and new systems run simultaneously
2. **Real-time validation**: Compare migrated data immediately
3. **Incremental verification**: Validate each batch before next
4. **Business process testing**: Key workflows work with migrated data
5. **Rollback testing**: Can revert if issues found

**Key question**: "Is the migration working RIGHT NOW?"

**Phase 3: Post-Migration Testing (The Review)**
**Goal**: Prove migration success and monitor for issues

**Activities:**
1. **Completeness verification**: 100% of data accounted for
2. **Accuracy verification**: 100% of fields correct
3. **Business validation**: All reports, processes, integrations work
4. **Performance benchmarking**: New system meets SLAs
5. **Monitoring setup**: Alerts for data quality issues
6. **Cleanup verification**: Old data properly archived/removed

**Key question**: "Can we declare success with confidence?"

**The testing progression:**
• **Pre-migration**: Test with samples (1%, 10%, 100% of production volume)
• **During migration**: Test with actual data as it migrates
• **Post-migration**: Test everything with full production data

Each phase builds confidence. Each verification adds certainty. By the time you're done, you don't just think migration worked. You KNOW it worked.

content.title: The Golden Rule of Migration Testing
content.explanation:
**Never migrate data you haven't first validated.**

This seems obvious, but it's violated constantly. Teams rush to move data, assuming validation will happen later. It doesn't. Or it happens too late.

**The validation-first approach:**

1. **Validate the source**: Know exactly what you're starting with
2. **Validate the destination**: Ensure it can hold everything correctly
3. **Validate the transformation**: Prove each data change is correct
4. **Validate the process**: Show migration works end-to-end
5. **Validate the result**: Confirm everything arrived intact

**What validation means in practice:**

```sql
-- BEFORE any migration:
-- 1. Understand source data quality
SELECT 
    COUNT(*) as total_records,
    COUNT(DISTINCT email) as unique_emails,
    SUM(CASE WHEN email IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as null_emails,
    MIN(created_at) as earliest_record,
    MAX(created_at) as latest_record
FROM legacy.users;

-- 2. Test transformation logic
SELECT 
    old_status,
    COUNT(*) as count,
    -- Show what new_status will be
    CASE old_status
        WHEN 'A' THEN 'ACTIVE'
        WHEN 'I' THEN 'INACTIVE'
        WHEN 'S' THEN 'SUSPENDED'
        ELSE 'UNKNOWN'
    END as new_status
FROM legacy.users
GROUP BY old_status;

-- 3. Verify destination can handle it
-- Check data type compatibility
-- Check constraints won't reject data
-- Check indexes exist for performance
```

**The validation mindset shift:**
Don't think: "We'll migrate, then check if it worked."
Think: "We'll prove it will work, then migrate."

Because in data migration, checking after is too late. The damage is done. The broken data is in production. The business is affected.

Validate first. Migrate second. Always.

content.title: The Migration Testing Toolkit: Practical Techniques
Completeness Testing: The Art of Counting Everything
content.explanation:
Completeness testing answers: "Did ALL the data make it?"

It sounds simple—just count records. But in real migrations, completeness is nuanced:

**What completeness really means:**
1. **Record completeness**: All records migrated
2. **Field completeness**: All fields in each record migrated
3. **Relationship completeness**: All relationships preserved
4. **Historical completeness**: All historical versions migrated
5. **Metadata completeness**: Timestamps, audit trails, versions migrated

**Completeness testing techniques:**

**Technique 1: Row counts (basic but essential)**
```sql
-- Table-level counts
SELECT 
    'users' as table_name,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy.users) as source_count,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.users) as dest_count,
    CASE 
        WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy.users) = 
             (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.users)
        THEN '✓ Complete'
        ELSE '✗ Incomplete'
    END as status;

-- With breakdown by status/category
SELECT 
    status,
    src.count as source_count,
    dst.count as dest_count,
    src.count - dst.count as difference
FROM (
    SELECT status, COUNT(*) as count
    FROM legacy.users
    GROUP BY status
) src
FULL OUTER JOIN (
    SELECT status, COUNT(*) as count
    FROM new_system.users
    GROUP BY status
) dst ON src.status = dst.status
WHERE src.count != dst.count OR src.count IS NULL OR dst.count IS NULL;
```

**Technique 2: ID range verification**
```sql
-- Verify all IDs from source exist in destination
SELECT 
    MIN(id) as min_id,
    MAX(id) as max_id,
    COUNT(DISTINCT id) as distinct_ids
FROM legacy.users
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT legacy_id FROM new_system.users);
-- Should return 0 rows
```

**Technique 3: Sampling verification**
```sql
-- For very large tables, verify samples
WITH random_sample AS (
    SELECT id
    FROM legacy.users
    TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM(1)  -- 1% random sample
    LIMIT 1000
)
SELECT 
    COUNT(*) as sample_size,
    SUM(CASE WHEN dest.id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as found_in_dest,
    ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN dest.id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) as completeness_percent
FROM random_sample src
LEFT JOIN new_system.users dest ON src.id = dest.legacy_id;
```

**Common completeness pitfalls:**
• **Counting wrong tables**: Migrated to different table structure
• **Missing archived data**: Only migrating 'active' records
• **Ignoring soft deletes**: Forgetting to migrate deleted records
• **Batch overlaps**: Some records migrated twice, others not at all
• **Timing gaps**: Data created during migration not captured

Completeness testing isn't just about numbers matching. It's about understanding WHAT should be counted, HOW it should be counted, and WHY discrepancies matter.

content.title: Accuracy Testing: When Close Enough Isn't Good Enough
content.explanation:
Accuracy testing answers: "Is the migrated data CORRECT?"

A record can be complete (exists in destination) but inaccurate (wrong values). Accuracy failures are often more dangerous than completeness failures because they're harder to detect.

**Types of accuracy failures:**

1. **Simple value errors**: `price = 19.99` → `price = 1999` (missing decimal)
2. **Format errors**: `date = '2024-01-15'` → `date = '15/01/2024'`
3. **Transformation errors**: `status = 'A'` → `status = 'Active'` (should be 'ACTIVE')
4. **Calculation errors**: `total = subtotal * 1.1` (wrong tax rate)
5. **Encoding errors**: `name = 'José'` → `name = 'JosÃ©'`
6. **Timezone errors**: `timestamp = '2024-01-15 14:30 UTC'` → `timestamp = '2024-01-15 14:30 EST'`

**Accuracy testing techniques:**

**Technique 1: Field-by-field comparison**
```sql
-- Compare every field for every record (for critical tables)
SELECT 
    src.id,
    'username mismatch' as issue,
    src.username as source_value,
    dest.username as dest_value
FROM legacy.users src
JOIN new_system.users dest ON src.id = dest.legacy_id
WHERE src.username != dest.username

UNION ALL

SELECT 
    src.id,
    'email mismatch',
    src.email,
    dest.email
FROM legacy.users src
JOIN new_system.users dest ON src.id = dest.legacy_id
WHERE src.email != dest.email

UNION ALL

-- Date comparison with tolerance
SELECT 
    src.id,
    'created_at mismatch',
    src.created_at::text,
    dest.created_at::text
FROM legacy.users src
JOIN new_system.users dest ON src.id = dest.legacy_id
WHERE ABS(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (src.created_at - dest.created_at))) > 1;  -- 1 second tolerance
```

**Technique 2: Business rule validation**
```sql
-- Verify migrated data follows business rules
-- Example: All prices must be positive
SELECT 
    'Negative prices' as rule_violation,
    COUNT(*) as violation_count
FROM new_system.products
WHERE price < 0;
-- Should return 0

-- Example: Email format validation
SELECT 
    'Invalid emails' as rule_violation,
    email,
    COUNT(*) as count
FROM new_system.users
WHERE email NOT LIKE '%@%.%'
GROUP BY email;
-- Should return 0 rows
```

**Technique 3: Checksum verification**
```sql
-- Generate checksums for data groups
WITH source_checksums AS (
    SELECT 
        status,
        COUNT(*) as record_count,
        SUM(MD5(username || email)::bit(32)::bigint) as data_hash
    FROM legacy.users
    GROUP BY status
),
dest_checksums AS (
    SELECT 
        status,
        COUNT(*) as record_count,
        SUM(MD5(username || email)::bit(32)::bigint) as data_hash
    FROM new_system.users
    GROUP BY status
)
SELECT 
    COALESCE(s.status, d.status) as status,
    s.record_count as source_count,
    d.record_count as dest_count,
    s.data_hash as source_hash,
    d.data_hash as dest_hash,
    CASE 
        WHEN s.record_count = d.record_count AND s.data_hash = d.data_hash 
        THEN '✓ Perfect match'
        WHEN s.record_count = d.record_count AND s.data_hash != d.data_hash 
        THEN '✗ Same count, different data'
        WHEN s.record_count != d.record_count AND s.data_hash = d.data_hash 
        THEN '✗ Different count, same hash (unlikely)'
        ELSE '✗ Different count and data'
    END as verification_status
FROM source_checksums s
FULL OUTER JOIN dest_checksums d ON s.status = d.status
WHERE s.record_count != d.record_count OR s.data_hash != d.data_hash;
```

**Accuracy testing requires understanding:**
• What transformations SHOULD happen
• What business rules MUST be preserved
• What tolerances are acceptable (dates within 1 second? amounts within 0.01?)
• What constitutes 'same meaning' vs 'same value'

Because in migration, 'technically correct' isn't enough. The data must be 'business correct.'

content.title: Relationship Testing: Keeping Data Families Together
content.explanation:
Data doesn't live in isolation. It has relationships—parents, children, siblings. When you migrate data, you're moving entire families. If relationships break, the data becomes meaningless.

**Types of relationships to test:**

1. **Parent-child**: Order → Order items
2. **Many-to-many**: Users ↔ Products (through purchases)
3. **Self-referencing**: Employee → Manager (who is also an employee)
4. **Cross-system**: User in CRM → Account in billing system
5. **Historical**: Current record → Previous versions

**Relationship testing techniques:**

**Technique 1: Foreign key verification**
```sql
-- Check that all foreign keys still point to valid records
SELECT 
    'Orphaned order items' as issue_type,
    COUNT(*) as orphan_count
FROM new_system.order_items oi
LEFT JOIN new_system.orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
-- Should be 0

-- Check relationship cardinality preserved
SELECT 
    'Orders with no items' as issue_type,
    COUNT(*) as count
FROM new_system.orders o
LEFT JOIN new_system.order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
WHERE oi.id IS NULL
  AND o.status != 'cancelled';  -- Cancelled orders might have no items
-- Should be 0 (or follow business rules)
```

**Technique 2: Many-to-many relationship verification**
```sql
-- Verify user-product purchase relationships
WITH source_relationships AS (
    SELECT 
        u.id as user_id,
        p.id as product_id,
        COUNT(*) as purchase_count
    FROM legacy.users u
    JOIN legacy.orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
    JOIN legacy.order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
    JOIN legacy.products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
    GROUP BY u.id, p.id
),
dest_relationships AS (
    SELECT 
        u.legacy_id as user_id,
        p.legacy_id as product_id,
        COUNT(*) as purchase_count
    FROM new_system.users u
    JOIN new_system.orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
    JOIN new_system.order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
    JOIN new_system.products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
    GROUP BY u.legacy_id, p.legacy_id
)
SELECT 
    COALESCE(s.user_id, d.user_id) as user_id,
    COALESCE(s.product_id, d.product_id) as product_id,
    s.purchase_count as source_count,
    d.purchase_count as dest_count,
    CASE 
        WHEN s.purchase_count = d.purchase_count THEN '✓ Match'
        WHEN s.purchase_count IS NULL THEN '✗ Missing in source'
        WHEN d.purchase_count IS NULL THEN '✗ Missing in destination'
        ELSE '✗ Count mismatch'
    END as status
FROM source_relationships s
FULL OUTER JOIN dest_relationships d 
    ON s.user_id = d.user_id AND s.product_id = d.product_id
WHERE s.purchase_count != d.purchase_count 
   OR s.purchase_count IS NULL 
   OR d.purchase_count IS NULL;
```

**Technique 3: Hierarchical data verification**
```sql
-- Verify organizational hierarchy preserved
WITH RECURSIVE source_hierarchy AS (
    SELECT id, manager_id, name, 1 as level
    FROM legacy.employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL  -- Start with top-level
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, e.name, sh.level + 1
    FROM legacy.employees e
    JOIN source_hierarchy sh ON e.manager_id = sh.id
),
dest_hierarchy AS (
    SELECT legacy_id, legacy_manager_id, name, 1 as level
    FROM new_system.employees
    WHERE legacy_manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.legacy_id, e.legacy_manager_id, e.name, dh.level + 1
    FROM new_system.employees e
    JOIN dest_hierarchy dh ON e.legacy_manager_id = dh.legacy_id
)
SELECT 
    'Hierarchy depth mismatch' as issue,
    (SELECT MAX(level) FROM source_hierarchy) as source_depth,
    (SELECT MAX(level) FROM dest_hierarchy) as dest_depth
WHERE (SELECT MAX(level) FROM source_hierarchy) != 
      (SELECT MAX(level) FROM dest_hierarchy);
```

**Common relationship failures:**
• **Orphaned children**: Order items without orders
• **Circular references**: Manager hierarchy loops
• **Broken many-to-many**: User-product links missing
• **Inconsistent references**: Foreign keys point to wrong table
• **Missing transitive relationships**: A→B→C, but A→C missing

Relationship testing ensures data arrives as a coherent whole, not as disconnected fragments. Because data without relationships is just noise.

content.title: Performance Testing: Will It Scale or Will It Fail?
content.explanation:
Migration isn't just about moving data. It's about moving data in a way that the new system can USE it. Performance testing answers: "Can the new system handle the migrated data?"

**Performance aspects to test:**

1. **Migration speed**: Can we complete within the downtime window?
2. **Query performance**: Are common queries still fast?
3. **Concurrency**: Can multiple users work simultaneously?
4. **Resource usage**: CPU, memory, disk I/O within limits?
5. **Index efficiency**: Do indexes work with migrated data?

**Performance testing techniques:**

**Technique 1: Migration speed benchmarking**
```sql
-- Measure migration performance
-- Before migration:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE 
INSERT INTO new_system.users 
SELECT * FROM legacy.users 
WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 10000;  -- Test with 10k records

-- Check execution time, plan efficiency
-- Scale up: 100k, 1M records to estimate full migration time

-- Monitor resource usage during test
SELECT 
    pg_stat_get_backend_pid(s.backendid) as pid,
    pg_stat_get_backend_activity(s.backendid) as query,
    pg_stat_get_backend_waiting(s.backendid) as waiting
FROM pg_stat_get_backend_idset() as s;
```

**Technique 2: Query performance comparison**
```sql
-- Compare query performance between old and new
-- Old system benchmark
	SELECT 
    'Old system' as system,
    query_name,
    AVG(execution_time_ms) as avg_time_ms,
    MAX(execution_time_ms) as max_time_ms,
    COUNT(*) as execution_count
FROM old_system.query_log
WHERE query_name IN ('get_user_orders', 'search_products', 'monthly_report')
  AND execution_date > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days'
GROUP BY query_name;

-- New system (after migration) benchmark
	SELECT 
    'New system' as system,
    query_name,
    AVG(execution_time_ms) as avg_time_ms,
    MAX(execution_time_ms) as max_time_ms,
    COUNT(*) as execution_count
FROM new_system.query_log
WHERE query_name IN ('get_user_orders', 'search_products', 'monthly_report')
GROUP BY query_name;

-- Compare: New system should be similar or better
```

**Technique 3: Concurrent access testing**
```sql
-- Simulate multiple users accessing migrated data
-- Create test script that:
-- 1. Starts 50 concurrent sessions
-- 2. Each session performs typical operations
-- 3. Measures response times
-- 4. Checks for deadlocks or timeouts

-- Example concurrent operations:
-- User 1-10: Browse products, add to cart
-- User 11-20: Search, filter, sort
-- User 21-30: Check orders, update profiles
-- User 31-40: Generate reports
-- User 41-50: Admin operations

-- Monitor with:
SELECT 
    COUNT(DISTINCT pid) as active_sessions,
    COUNT(*) as total_queries,
    AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (query_end - query_start))) as avg_query_time
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active';
```

**Common performance issues:**
• **Missing indexes**: Queries that were fast become slow
• **Wrong data types**: Text where should be enum, causing slow comparisons
• **Inefficient schema**: Normalization/denormalization issues
• **Resource contention**: Too many connections, locking
• **Network latency**: Cross-region data access slows queries

Performance testing ensures migrated data doesn't just exist—it works. Because data that's technically correct but practically unusable is still a failure.

content.title: The Retail Migration That Brought Down Black Friday
content.scenario: Major retailer migrates inventory system before holiday season
content.outcome: Website crashes on Black Friday, loses $15M in sales
content.details: Inventory system migrated successfully → All data verified correct → Black Friday 8:00 AM: 100,000 concurrent users → Product search queries timeout → Shopping cart updates fail → Checkout process hangs → Root cause: Migrated product table missing composite index on (category_id, price) → Queries that took 50ms now take 5 seconds → Database connections exhausted → 4-hour outage during peak sales → Fix: Emergency index creation → Too late, customers already left

content.caption: Comprehensive Migration Validation Framework
content.code:
-- ============================================
-- COMPREHENSIVE MIGRATION VALIDATION FRAMEWORK
-- Run this after migration to verify everything
-- ============================================

-- Create validation results table
CREATE TABLE migration_validation_results (
    validation_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    validation_category VARCHAR(50),
    validation_name VARCHAR(100),
    check_description TEXT,
    source_value NUMERIC,
    destination_value NUMERIC,
    difference NUMERIC,
    status VARCHAR(20),
    validation_timestamp TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- 1. COMPLETENESS CHECKS
-- Record counts for all major tables
INSERT INTO migration_validation_results 
    (validation_category, validation_name, check_description, 
     source_value, destination_value, difference, status)
SELECT 
    'Completeness' as category,
    'Record count: ' || table_name as validation_name,
    'Total records in table' as description,
    source_count,
    dest_count,
    source_count - dest_count as difference,
    CASE 
        WHEN source_count = dest_count THEN 'PASS'
        ELSE 'FAIL'
    END as status
FROM (
    VALUES 
        ('users', 
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy.users),
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.users)),
        ('products', 
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy.products),
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.products)),
        ('orders', 
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy.orders),
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.orders))
    -- Add all tables here
) as tables(table_name, source_count, dest_count);

-- 2. ACCURACY CHECKS
-- Sample record comparison
WITH sample_users AS (
    SELECT id, username, email, created_at
    FROM legacy.users
    WHERE MOD(id, 1000) = 0  -- 0.1% sample
    LIMIT 100
)
INSERT INTO migration_validation_results 
    (validation_category, validation_name, check_description,
     source_value, destination_value, difference, status)
SELECT 
    'Accuracy' as category,
    'Field accuracy: users' as validation_name,
    'Compare sample user records' as description,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sample_users) as source_value,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sample_users s
     JOIN new_system.users n ON s.id = n.legacy_id
     WHERE s.username = n.username 
       AND s.email = n.email
       AND ABS(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (s.created_at - n.created_at))) <= 1) as dest_value,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sample_users) - 
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sample_users s
     JOIN new_system.users n ON s.id = n.legacy_id
     WHERE s.username = n.username 
       AND s.email = n.email
       AND ABS(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (s.created_at - n.created_at))) <= 1) as difference,
    CASE 
        WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sample_users) = 
             (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sample_users s
              JOIN new_system.users n ON s.id = n.legacy_id
              WHERE s.username = n.username 
                AND s.email = n.email
                AND ABS(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (s.created_at - n.created_at))) <= 1)
        THEN 'PASS'
        ELSE 'FAIL'
    END as status;

-- 3. RELATIONSHIP CHECKS
-- Foreign key integrity
INSERT INTO migration_validation_results 
    (validation_category, validation_name, check_description,
     source_value, destination_value, difference, status)
SELECT 
    'Relationships' as category,
    'Orphaned order items' as validation_name,
    'Order items without valid orders' as description,
    0 as source_value,  -- Should be 0 in both systems
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.order_items oi
     LEFT JOIN new_system.orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
     WHERE o.id IS NULL) as destination_value,
    - (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.order_items oi
       LEFT JOIN new_system.orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
       WHERE o.id IS NULL) as difference,
    CASE 
        WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.order_items oi
              LEFT JOIN new_system.orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
              WHERE o.id IS NULL) = 0
        THEN 'PASS'
        ELSE 'FAIL'
    END as status;

-- 4. BUSINESS RULE CHECKS
-- Validate critical business rules
INSERT INTO migration_validation_results 
    (validation_category, validation_name, check_description,
     source_value, destination_value, difference, status)
SELECT 
    'Business Rules' as category,
    'Negative prices' as validation_name,
    'Products with negative prices' as description,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy.products WHERE price < 0) as source_value,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.products WHERE price < 0) as destination_value,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy.products WHERE price < 0) - 
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.products WHERE price < 0) as difference,
    CASE 
        WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_system.products WHERE price < 0) = 0
        THEN 'PASS'
        ELSE 'FAIL'
    END as status;

-- 5. GENERATE VALIDATION REPORT
SELECT 
    validation_category,
    validation_name,
    check_description,
    source_value,
    destination_value,
    difference,
    status,
    CASE 
        WHEN status = 'PASS' THEN '✅'
        ELSE '❌'
    END as status_icon
FROM migration_validation_results
ORDER BY validation_category, validation_name;

-- Calculate overall success rate
SELECT 
    'Overall Migration Validation' as summary,
    COUNT(*) as total_checks,
    SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'PASS' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as passed_checks,
    SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'FAIL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as failed_checks,
    ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'PASS' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) as success_rate
FROM migration_validation_results;

-- ============================================
-- This framework provides:
-- 1. Systematic validation of all migration aspects
-- 2. Clear pass/fail status for each check
-- 3. Quantitative metrics for success
-- 4. Audit trail of validation results
-- 5. Executive summary for stakeholders
-- ============================================

content.caption: Automated Migration Testing Script
content.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Automated Data Migration Testing Framework
Validates migration completeness, accuracy, and integrity
"""

import psycopg2
import time
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple
from dataclasses import dataclass
import hashlib

@dataclass
class MigrationTestResult:
    test_category: str
    test_name: str
    passed: bool
    details: str
    source_value: any = None
    dest_value: any = None
    execution_time_ms: float = 0.0

class MigrationValidator:
    def __init__(self, source_conn_str: str, dest_conn_str: str):
        self.source_conn = psycopg2.connect(source_conn_str)
        self.dest_conn = psycopg2.connect(dest_conn_str)
        self.results: List[MigrationTestResult] = []
    
    def test_record_counts(self, table_pairs: List[Tuple[str, str]]) -> List[MigrationTestResult]:
        """Test that record counts match between source and destination"""
        results = []
        
        for source_table, dest_table in table_pairs:
            start_time = time.time()
            
            try:
                # Get source count
                with self.source_conn.cursor() as cur:
                    cur.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {source_table}")
                    source_count = cur.fetchone()[0]
                
                # Get destination count
                with self.dest_conn.cursor() as cur:
                    cur.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {dest_table}")
                    dest_count = cur.fetchone()[0]
                
                passed = source_count == dest_count
                details = f"Source: {source_count:,}, Destination: {dest_count:,}"
                
            except Exception as e:
                passed = False
                details = f"Error: {e}"
                source_count = dest_count = 0
            
            results.append(MigrationTestResult(
                test_category="Completeness",
                test_name=f"Record count: {source_table} → {dest_table}",
                passed=passed,
                details=details,
                source_value=source_count,
                dest_value=dest_count,
                execution_time_ms=(time.time() - start_time) * 1000
            ))
        
        return results
    
    def test_data_accuracy(self, table_name: str, id_column: str, sample_size: int = 100) -> MigrationTestResult:
        """Test data accuracy by comparing sample records"""
        start_time = time.time()
        
        try:
            # Get sample IDs from source
            with self.source_conn.cursor() as cur:
                cur.execute(f"""
                    SELECT {id_column} 
                    FROM {table_name} 
                    WHERE {id_column} % 1000 = 0  -- Sample pattern
                    ORDER BY RANDOM() 
                    LIMIT %s
                """, (sample_size,))
                sample_ids = [row[0] for row in cur.fetchall()]
            
            if not sample_ids:
                return MigrationTestResult(
                    test_category="Accuracy",
                    test_name=f"Data accuracy: {table_name}",
                    passed=False,
                    details="No sample IDs found",
                    execution_time_ms=(time.time() - start_time) * 1000
                )
            
            # Compare each sample record
            mismatches = []
            for sample_id in sample_ids:
                # Get source record
                with self.source_conn.cursor() as cur:
                    cur.execute(f"""
                        SELECT * FROM {table_name} 
                        WHERE {id_column} = %s
                    """, (sample_id,))
                    source_record = cur.fetchone()
                    source_cols = [desc[0] for desc in cur.description]
                
                # Get destination record
                with self.dest_conn.cursor() as cur:
                    cur.execute(f"""
                        SELECT * FROM {table_name} 
                        WHERE legacy_{id_column} = %s
                    """, (sample_id,))
                    dest_record = cur.fetchone()
                
                if not dest_record:
                    mismatches.append(f"ID {sample_id}: Not found in destination")
                    continue
                
                # Compare fields (skip legacy_id column)
                for i, col in enumerate(source_cols):
                    if col == id_column:
                        continue  # Skip ID comparison (different in dest)
                    
                    source_val = source_record[i]
                    dest_val = dest_record[i]
                    
                    # Handle None values
                    if source_val is None and dest_val is None:
                        continue
                    if source_val is None or dest_val is None:
                        mismatches.append(f"ID {sample_id}.{col}: NULL mismatch")
                        continue
                    
                    # Compare values
                    if str(source_val) != str(dest_val):
                        # For dates, allow small differences
                        if isinstance(source_val, datetime) and isinstance(dest_val, datetime):
                            diff = abs((source_val - dest_val).total_seconds())
                            if diff > 1:  # 1 second tolerance
                                mismatches.append(f"ID {sample_id}.{col}: Date mismatch ({diff}s)")
                        else:
                            mismatches.append(f"ID {sample_id}.{col}: '{source_val}' != '{dest_val}'")
            
            passed = len(mismatches) == 0
            details = f"Compared {len(sample_ids)} records"
            if mismatches:
                details += f", {len(mismatches)} mismatches: {', '.join(mismatches[:3])}"
                if len(mismatches) > 3:
                    details += f"... and {len(mismatches) - 3} more"
            
        except Exception as e:
            passed = False
            details = f"Error: {e}"
        
        return MigrationTestResult(
            test_category="Accuracy",
            test_name=f"Data accuracy: {table_name}",
            passed=passed,
            details=details,
            execution_time_ms=(time.time() - start_time) * 1000
        )
    
    def test_relationships(self) -> List[MigrationTestResult]:
        """Test that relationships are preserved"""
        results = []
        
        # Test 1: Orphaned order items
        start_time = time.time()
        try:
            with self.dest_conn.cursor() as cur:
                cur.execute("""
                    SELECT COUNT(*) 
                    FROM order_items oi
                    LEFT JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
                    WHERE o.id IS NULL
                """)
                orphan_count = cur.fetchone()[0]
            
            passed = orphan_count == 0
            details = f"Found {orphan_count} orphaned order items"
            
        except Exception as e:
            passed = False
            details = f"Error: {e}"
            orphan_count = 0
        
        results.append(MigrationTestResult(
            test_category="Relationships",
            test_name="Orphaned order items",
            passed=passed,
            details=details,
            dest_value=orphan_count,
            execution_time_ms=(time.time() - start_time) * 1000
        ))
        
        # Test 2: Users without profiles
        start_time = time.time()
        try:
            with self.dest_conn.cursor() as cur:
                cur.execute("""
                    SELECT COUNT(*) 
                    FROM users u
                    LEFT JOIN user_profiles up ON u.id = up.user_id
                    WHERE up.id IS NULL
                      AND u.status = 'active'
                """)
                users_without_profiles = cur.fetchone()[0]
            
            # Business rule: Active users should have profiles
            passed = users_without_profiles == 0
            details = f"Found {users_without_profiles} active users without profiles"
            
        except Exception as e:
            passed = False
            details = f"Error: {e}"
            users_without_profiles = 0
        
        results.append(MigrationTestResult(
            test_category="Relationships",
            test_name="Users without profiles",
            passed=passed,
            details=details,
            dest_value=users_without_profiles,
            execution_time_ms=(time.time() - start_time) * 1000
        ))
        
        return results
    
    def run_comprehensive_validation(self) -> Dict[str, any]:
        """Run all validation tests"""
        print("🚀 Starting Comprehensive Migration Validation\n")
        
        # Run all test suites
        all_results = []
        
        print("📊 Testing Completeness (Record Counts)...")
        table_pairs = [
            ("users", "users"),
            ("products", "products"),
            ("orders", "orders"),
            ("order_items", "order_items")
        ]
        all_results.extend(self.test_record_counts(table_pairs))
        
        print("🎯 Testing Data Accuracy...")
        all_results.append(self.test_data_accuracy("users", "id", 50))
        all_results.append(self.test_data_accuracy("products", "id", 30))
        
        print("🔗 Testing Relationships...")
        all_results.extend(self.test_relationships())
        
        # Calculate statistics
        total_tests = len(all_results)
        passed_tests = sum(1 for r in all_results if r.passed)
        failed_tests = total_tests - passed_tests
        success_rate = (passed_tests / total_tests * 100) if total_tests > 0 else 0
        
        # Generate report
        print("\n📈 VALIDATION REPORT:")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        # Group by category
        categories = {}
        for result in all_results:
            if result.test_category not in categories:
                categories[result.test_category] = []
            categories[result.test_category].append(result)
        
        for category, category_results in categories.items():
            print(f"\n{category.upper()}:")
            print("-" * 40)
            
            category_passed = sum(1 for r in category_results if r.passed)
            category_total = len(category_results)
            
            for result in category_results:
                status = "✅ PASS" if result.passed else "❌ FAIL"
                print(f"{status} {result.test_name}")
                print(f"   {result.details}")
                if result.execution_time_ms > 0:
                    print(f"   Time: {result.execution_time_ms:.1f}ms")
                print()
            
            print(f"Category Summary: {category_passed}/{category_total} passed")
        
        print("=" * 80)
        print(f"\n🎯 OVERALL RESULTS: {passed_tests}/{total_tests} tests passed ({success_rate:.1f}%)")
        
        if passed_tests == total_tests:
            print("🌟 Migration validation SUCCESSFUL!")
        else:
            print(f"⚠️  Migration validation FAILED: {failed_tests} issues found")
            
            # Show failed tests
            print("\n❌ FAILED TESTS:")
            for result in all_results:
                if not result.passed:
                    print(f"• {result.test_name}: {result.details}")
        
        return {
            "total_tests": total_tests,
            "passed_tests": passed_tests,
            "failed_tests": failed_tests,
            "success_rate": success_rate,
            "results": all_results
        }
    
    def close(self):
        """Close database connections"""
        self.source_conn.close()
        self.dest_conn.close()

# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Configuration
    SOURCE_DB = "host=localhost dbname=legacy_system user=test"
    DEST_DB = "host=localhost dbname=new_system user=test"
    
    # Create validator
    validator = MigrationValidator(SOURCE_DB, DEST_DB)
    
    try:
        # Run validation
        results = validator.run_comprehensive_validation()
        
        # Save results to file
        with open("migration_validation_report.txt", "w") as f:
            f.write(f"Migration Validation Report\n")
            f.write(f"Generated: {datetime.now()}\n\n")
            f.write(f"Overall: {results['passed_tests']}/{results['total_tests']} passed ({results['success_rate']:.1f}%)\n\n")
            
            for result in results["results"]:
                status = "PASS" if result.passed else "FAIL"
                f.write(f"{status}: {result.test_category} - {result.test_name}\n")
                f.write(f"  {result.details}\n\n")
        
        print(f"\n📄 Report saved to: migration_validation_report.txt")
        
    finally:
        validator.close()
    
    # Exit with appropriate code
    if results["success_rate"] == 100:
        exit(0)  # Success
    else:
        exit(1)  # Failure

content.title: The Migration Testing Lifecycle
content.explanation:
Migration testing isn't a one-time event. It's a continuous lifecycle that begins long before migration and continues long after.

**Phase 1: Planning & Preparation (Months Before)**
• **Data profiling**: Understand source data structure, quality, relationships
• **Risk assessment**: Identify critical data, business processes, dependencies
• **Test strategy**: Define what to test, how to test, success criteria
• **Tool selection**: Choose validation tools, monitoring systems
• **Environment setup**: Create test environments mirroring production

**Phase 2: Development & Unit Testing (Weeks Before)**
• **Transformation testing**: Unit test each data transformation
• **Migration script testing**: Test extraction, transformation, loading scripts
• **Performance testing**: Test with production-sized data subsets
• **Error handling testing**: Test rollback, recovery procedures
• **Integration testing**: Test with dependent systems

**Phase 3: Dry Runs & Dress Rehearsals (Days Before)**
• **Full-scale dry run**: Complete migration on test environment
• **Parallel run testing**: Compare old and new system outputs
• **Business validation**: Key users verify migrated data works
• **Performance validation**: Verify SLAs met with migrated data
• **Rollback testing**: Practice reverting if issues found

**Phase 4: Production Migration (The Event)**
• **Real-time validation**: Monitor migration progress, validate each batch
• **Incremental verification**: Verify subsets before moving to next
• **Business process testing**: Critical paths tested immediately
• **Issue response**: Quick validation of any issues found
• **Go/no-go decisions**: Data-driven decisions at each milestone

**Phase 5: Post-Migration & Monitoring (Weeks After)**
• **Comprehensive validation**: 100% data verification
• **Business acceptance**: All departments sign off
• **Performance monitoring**: Track system performance with real load
• **Data quality monitoring**: Ongoing checks for data integrity
• **Cleanup verification**: Old systems properly decommissioned

**Phase 6: Lessons Learned & Documentation (Ongoing)**
• **Post-mortem analysis**: What worked, what didn't
• **Documentation update**: Update runbooks, procedures
• **Knowledge transfer**: Share lessons with organization
• **Tool improvement**: Enhance testing frameworks
• **Process refinement**: Improve for next migration

**The continuous testing mindset:**
Migration testing never really ends. It evolves:
• **Before migration**: "Will it work?"
• **During migration**: "Is it working?"
• **After migration**: "Did it work?"
• **Long after**: "Is it still working?"

Your testing adapts to each phase. Your rigor increases as you get closer to production. Your verification becomes more comprehensive as risks materialize.

Because successful migration isn't just about moving data. It's about maintaining confidence throughout the journey.

content.title: The Migration Tester's Manifesto
content.explanation:
**We test migrations because:**

1. **Data is memory** - It's the history of our business
2. **Migrations are irreversible** - There's no undo button for bad data
3. **Trust is fragile** - One migration failure can destroy years of trust
4. **Costs are real** - Every migration error has a price tag
5. **Success is binary** - Migrations either work perfectly or fail completely

**Our testing principles:**

1. **Verify, don't assume** - Check every record, every field, every relationship
2. **Test early, test often** - Find issues when they're cheap to fix
3. **Think like the business** - What data matters most to operations?
4. **Prepare for failure** - Have rollback plans, have monitoring, have alerts
5. **Document everything** - What we tested, what we found, what we fixed
6. **Communicate clearly** - Status, risks, issues in business language
7. **Automate rigorously** - Consistent, repeatable validation
8. **Measure everything** - Counts, percentages, success rates, confidence levels

**Our success criteria:**
Not when the migration completes.
Not when the data verifies.
Not when the business signs off.

Our success is when, six months later, no one remembers the migration happened because everything just works.

When reports run without issues.
When customers find their history intact.
When business processes flow smoothly.
When the new system feels like it was always there.

That's the goal. Not just moved data. Preserved trust. Maintained continuity. Sustained operations.

Start with one table. Validate it completely. Learn the patterns. Build confidence. Then tackle the next.

Because in migration testing, perfection isn't a luxury. It's the only acceptable outcome.

And you're the guardian of that perfection. Welcome to the most important testing you'll ever do.

content.title: The Backup Reality Check: Why Most Backups Are Theater
The Great Backup Illusion
content.explanation: Every company has backups. Few companies have recoveries. Backup success messages lie—they say 'backup completed' but don't say 'backup is restorable.' When disaster strikes, 'mostly backed up' equals 'not backed up.' Real examples: GitLab's backup script deleting production data, Code Spaces losing all backups to hackers, MongoDB paying $50K ransom when backups were also encrypted.

content.title: The Cost of Untested Backups
content.explanation: Failed recovery costs: $5,600/minute downtime (Gartner), 40 hours to recreate 1 hour of lost data, GDPR fines up to €20M, 40% customer churn after data loss. Testing ROI: $15K/year testing prevents $400K+ losses. Backup tests aren't expenses—they're the cheapest insurance you'll buy.

content.caption: Basic Backup Verification Queries
content.code:
-- Backup completeness check
SELECT 
    schemaname,
    tablename,
    (SELECT MAX(backup_time) FROM backup_log WHERE table_name = t.tablename) as last_backup,
    EXTRACT(DAY FROM NOW() - (SELECT MAX(backup_time) FROM backup_log WHERE table_name = t.tablename)) as days_since,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM backup_validation WHERE table_name = t.tablename AND validation_type = 'row_count') as backup_count,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t.tablename) as current_count
FROM pg_tables t
WHERE schemaname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
  AND tablename IN ('users', 'orders', 'products', 'transactions')
ORDER BY days_since DESC NULLS FIRST;

-- Data integrity check
WITH source_sample AS (
    SELECT id, MD5(username || email || created_at::text) as record_hash
    FROM users WHERE id % 1000 = 0 LIMIT 100
),
backup_sample AS (
    SELECT id, MD5(username || email || created_at::text) as record_hash
    FROM backup_restore.users WHERE id % 1000 = 0 LIMIT 100
)
SELECT 
    'Data integrity' as test,
    COUNT(*) as total_samples,
    SUM(CASE WHEN s.record_hash = b.record_hash THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as matching,
    ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN s.record_hash = b.record_hash THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) as integrity_percent
FROM source_sample s JOIN backup_sample b ON s.id = b.id;

content.title: The RTO/RPO Testing Framework
content.explanation: RTO (Recovery Time Objective): 'How long can we be down?' RPO (Recovery Point Objective): 'How much data can we lose?' Test: 1) Baseline current capabilities, 2) Scenario testing (complete loss, corruption, partial loss), 3) Load testing (limited bandwidth/staff), 4) Continuous validation. RTO/RPO become survival thresholds during disasters.

content.title: The First Rule of Backup Testing
content.explanation: Never trust a backup you haven't restored. Verification mindset: Don't ask 'Is backup job successful?' Ask 'Can I run business from this backup?' Success metrics lie: 99.9% backup success = 8.76 hours/year failed backups. Mantra: 'I will restore before I trust. Verify before I rely. Test before I need.'

content.title: The Recovery Testing Toolkit: Practical Techniques
Completeness Testing: Did We Get Everything?
content.explanation: Test: 1) Data completeness (all databases/tables), 2) Configuration completeness (settings/files), 3) Code completeness (app/dependencies), 4) Security completeness (certificates/keys), 5) Metadata completeness (timestamps/checksums). Use inventory-based verification, checksum validation, dependency mapping.

content.title: Integrity Testing: Is the Data Still True?
content.explanation: Backup can be complete but corrupted. Test: 1) Checksum validation at file/database/record levels, 2) Sample comparison (0.1-1% random records), 3) Business rule validation (negative prices? future dates?), 4) Relationship integrity (foreign keys intact).

content.title: Point-in-Time Recovery Testing
content.explanation: Test restoring to specific timestamps (critical for ransomware, human errors). Challenges: 1) Transaction log consistency, 2) Dependent data state, 3) Application compatibility. Test methodology: 1) Create known state, 2) Simulate disaster, 3) Restore to timestamp, 4) Verify data/app state.

content.title: Disaster Scenario Testing
content.explanation: Test real-world scenarios: 1) Complete data center loss, 2) Ransomware encryption, 3) Accidental mass deletion, 4) Schema corruption, 5) Failed upgrades. Each scenario requires different recovery procedures. Test with increasing severity: table → database → server → data center.
